newsitem.title: ITALY: Ex-Nazi Priebke in court at start of new trial.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Nazi Priebke in court at start of new trial.

text.p: Former Nazi SS captain Erich Priebke, accused in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity, went on trial for the second time in a year on Monday but told the court he would only attend future hearings when necessary.

"I am here today out of respect for the tribunal," Priebke told the court in Rome's high-security Rebibbia prison. "But I fear it will not be this way in the future. I am available for whatever may be needed."

The military court decided, after retiring for more than two hours, to try the 83-year-old German together with Karl Hass, a former SS major accused in the same 1944 massacre of 335 men and boys, 75 of them Jews, in Rome's Ardeatine Caves.
Priebke, who is under house arrest at a Roman Catholic monastery south of Rome, is facing a re-trial while Hass, also under house arrest, is being tried for the first time.

Priebke was found guilty last August of involvement in the massacre in caves south of Rome but was ordered to be released under a statute of limitation. The verdict, which sparked a storm of protest, was quashed on appeal and a retrial ordered.
Both men admit to having taken part in the massacre, but say they were following orders and would have been executed if they had refused to act.
Under Italian law, defendants are not obliged to attend trial sessions, and Hass, whose lawyer said he was not well, was not present at the heavily guarded session.

Priebke, wearing a light grey suit, entered the room only after the court issued its ruling on joining the two cases. He gave his name and birthdate, on July 29, 1913 in Berlin, in Italian. The session was later adjourned until Thursday.

The former SS captain, who was extradited from Argentina in November 1995, admits he shot two victims in the massacre, which came as a reprisal for a partisan bomb attack in which 33 troops loyal to the Nazis died. He maintains it was an act of war.

Present in the stark prison courtroom was Shimon Samuels, Paris-based director of international affairs from the Simon Wiesenthal Center. He likened the trial to that of Klaus Barbie, head of the Lyon Gestapo who was sentenced to life imprisonment in France in 1987.

"This is the Italian Barbie trial...There are many aspects to this new trial which give a second chance to justice. We want satisfaction...for the families of the victims who have been waiting for 50 years in total frustration for justice."
Samuels said the trial came at an important moment for Italy and Europe.
"We feel it is the right moment for this trial and we think that it's extremely important," he said.
Priebke's first trial ended in uproar last August when the judge handed down the verdict freeing him.
Protesters besieged the courtroom stopping him from leaving until Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick ordered his re-arrest based on an extradition request by Germany.
The extradition request was later turned down but in the meantime the original verdict had been thrown out on appeal.

Dutch Roman Catholic priest Father Peter Van Meyl, who visited Priebke in the Franciscan monastery two days before the second trial, told reporters the former SS captain was nervous before the proceedings.
"Sure he's nervous. It's normal ... It's a sign that he's a person that's still alive," he said.
